# Prompting and In-Context Learning {#sec-prompting}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements here were run on the same
Turkish product-review corpus as @sec-bake-off and @sec-classification —
233,508 de-duplicated reviews — but on a **balanced** sample rather than the
natural 93.7%-positive distribution, so that accuracy is readable against a
50% floor and the effect being measured is the prompt rather than the class
prior. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `qwen3.5:9b`, Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain what in-context learning is and why putting examples in a prompt
  changes behaviour without changing a single weight;
- apply the pattern library — role, structure, demonstrations, decomposition —
  and say what each one is actually for;
- write a prompt as a *specification* with an output contract, rather than as
  a request;
- measure how much of your score is the prompt rather than the model, and
  build the evaluation that makes prompt changes reviewable.

## Why prompting works at all {#sec-prompting-why}

A pretrained model predicts the next token. Nothing in that objective says it
should follow an instruction, and the first large models mostly did not —
you had to trick them, by writing a prefix whose natural continuation happened
to be the answer you wanted. @reynolds2021prompt is the historical document
for that era, and reading it now is a good reminder of how much of "prompt
engineering" was working around a missing capability.

Two things changed. **Scale** made models able to infer a task from examples
in the context [@brown2020language], and **instruction tuning**
(@sec-post-training) trained them to treat an instruction as an instruction
rather than as text to continue. The second is why modern prompting feels like
asking rather than tricking.

::: {#gloss-in-context-learning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**in-context learning** (bağlam içi öğrenme) — the model doing better at a
task because examples of it are sitting in the prompt. No weight is updated
and nothing survives the call, which is why *learning* is a slightly
misleading word for it.
[↩](#term-in-context-learning){.term-back}
:::

[In-context learning](#gloss-in-context-learning){#term-in-context-learning .term-ref}
is the first of those: you put input-output pairs in the prompt, and the model
does better on the next input, **with no weight updated and nothing retained
after the call**. It is not learning in the sense @sec-post-training uses the
word. A better description is *task inference*: the examples narrow down which
of the many tasks the model already knows how to do you are asking for.

That framing predicts something odd, and the prediction holds.
@min2022rethinking replaced the labels in the demonstrations with **random**
ones and found performance mostly survived. What the examples were mainly
conveying was the *shape* of the task — the label space, the format, the
distribution of inputs — not the input-to-label mapping. That is worth
knowing before you spend a week curating perfect examples.

::: {.column-margin}
It also predicts the failure mode. If demonstrations mostly convey format,
then a model that already knows the format gains little from them — which is
exactly what @sec-classification measured, where eight examples were worth
+7.17 macro-F1 on one model and +0.51 ($p = 0.62$) on a stronger one. The
technique did not stop working; the models stopped needing it.
:::

### The claim this chapter is built on

[The prompt is part of the model.]{.hl} Not a message to it — a component of
the system, sitting in the same position a feature-extraction function sits in
@sec-bake-off's pipeline. It has a version, it has a contract, it has
regressions, and changing it changes your output distribution as surely as
swapping the checkpoint would.

The rest of the chapter is what follows from taking that seriously, and
@sec-prompting-brittle is the measurement that makes it hard to avoid.

## A pattern library {#sec-prompting-patterns}

Five patterns cover most of what works. They are not magic words; each one is
doing an identifiable job.

**Role.** *You are an experienced customer-feedback analyst.* The job is to
select a region of the model's distribution — vocabulary, register, what
counts as a relevant detail. It is weakest when it asks for expertise the
model does not have (a role prefix does not make a model a doctor) and
strongest when it disambiguates *style*, which is a real and frequent need.

**Structure.** Sections, delimiters, an explicit place for the input. The job
is to make the boundary between your instruction and the user's data
unambiguous — for the model, and for the injection-safety reasons
@sec-agent-security covers. `<review>...</review>` is not decoration; it is
the difference between data and instruction.

**Demonstrations.** Input-output pairs. The job, per @min2022rethinking, is
mainly to fix the *format and label space*. Use them when the output shape is
unusual or hard to describe, and expect less from them when the task is one
the model has obviously seen.

**Decomposition.** Ask for one thing at a time, or ask for intermediate
results before the answer. The job is to move work out of a single forward
pass and into tokens — which is @sec-reasoning's subject, and where the
measurement of when it helps lives. This chapter's contribution is the
practical corollary: **a prompt that asks for four things at once will do at
least one of them badly**, and splitting it is usually cheaper than fixing it.

**Output contract.** State the exact shape of the answer, and make it the
easiest thing for the model to produce. This is the pattern with the most
leverage and it gets its own section.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What about "think step by step"?

It belongs to @sec-reasoning, which measures it properly, and the short answer
is that the phrase is a relic. @kojima2022large found it worked on models that
had not been trained to reason; models that *have* been trained to reason
produce the trace whether or not you ask, and adding the phrase to a reasoning
model mostly wastes tokens.

The durable part is not the phrase but the mechanism: more tokens before the
answer means more computation available to produce it. Ask for intermediate
results when the task needs them, and skip the incantation.
:::

## Prompts as specifications {#sec-prompting-spec}

The most useful shift in this chapter is grammatical: stop writing prompts as
*requests* and start writing them as *specifications*.

A request says what you want. A specification says what a valid output is —
which means it can be checked, and a prompt whose output can be checked is a
prompt you can test.

```text
request         "Summarise the customer's complaint."

specification   "Return one JSON object with keys `issue` (string, max 15
                 words), `severity` (one of: low, medium, high) and
                 `product` (string, copied exactly from the review, or null
                 if no product is named). Return nothing else."
```

The second version gives you three things the first does not: a parser that
either succeeds or fails loudly, a set of values you can validate, and a
`null` that distinguishes *absent* from *unknown* — which is the distinction
@sec-sequence-labeling found LLM extractors quietly destroying.

Three rules that follow:

1. **Name the failure output.** If the model cannot comply, what should it
   return? A prompt without an escape hatch gets a fabricated answer instead
   of an admission, because you left the model no legal way to say no.
2. **Put the constraint where it binds.** An instruction 800 tokens above the
   input competes with the input for attention. Constraints that must hold go
   close to the end.
3. **Make the contract machine-checkable, then check it.** A schema you do not
   validate is a comment. @sec-decoding is where the enforcement machinery
   lives — grammars, JSON Schema, and the measurement of what constraining
   costs.

::: {.column-margin}
And a warning from @sec-summarization, which is worth repeating in the chapter
where the schema gets written rather than the one where it gets enforced: a
schema guarantees *shape*, never *truth*. A grammar-constrained call happily
returned `{"answer": 1}` for the capital of France. Validating the contract
tells you the output is well-formed and nothing else.
:::

## How much of your score is the prompt? {#sec-prompting-brittle}

Everything above is craft. This section is the measurement that makes the
craft matter, and it is the one to run on your own task before you trust any
number you have.

Twelve prompts were written for the same task — decide whether a Turkish
product review is positive or negative. **A competent reader would call them
the same instruction.** They differ in formatting, in the surface form of the
labels, in where the review sits relative to the instruction, in delimiters,
and in politeness. None changes the task, the criteria, or the meaning of
either label.

All twelve ran on the same 150 balanced reviews, same model, temperature 0,
fixed seed. Every response parsed; nothing was dropped.

```text
variant                        acc      95% CI (Wilson)
label positive/negative     90.00%   [ 84.2,  93.8]
label A/B                   88.67%   [ 82.6,  92.8]
bulleted                    87.33%   [ 81.1,  91.7]
numbered                    87.33%   [ 81.1,  91.7]
label 1/0                   86.67%   [ 80.3,  91.2]
triple quotes               82.00%   [ 75.1,  87.3]
baseline                    79.33%   [ 72.2,  85.0]
label olumlu/olumsuz        78.00%   [ 70.7,  83.9]
xml delimiters              77.33%   [ 70.0,  83.3]
polite                      76.67%   [ 69.3,  82.7]
role prefix                 76.00%   [ 68.6,  82.1]
review first                75.33%   [ 67.9,  81.5]

spread 75.33% – 90.00% = 14.67 points     mean 82.06   sd 5.57
```

::: {.anlp-widget}


```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`The dashed line is the plain \`baseline\` prompt. Note that the three
best variants differ from it *only* in how the two labels are spelled or how
```

[Fourteen and a half points of accuracy, between two prompts that say the same
thing.]{.hl}

### Is that real, or is it 150 documents of noise?

The confidence intervals overlap, so the obvious next question is whether any
of this survives contact with statistics. It does, because the comparison is
**paired** — the same documents through both prompts — and a paired test is far
more powerful than comparing two independent proportions.

```text
best  'label positive/negative'  90.00%
worst 'review first'             75.33%

  documents where they disagree            42
    best right, worst wrong                32
    worst right, best wrong                10
  McNemar exact test                    p = 0.0009
```

The difference is not noise. And the stronger statistic is the one that does
not involve accuracy at all:

```text
all 12 variants give the same answer on   104/150 = 69.3% of reviews
the prompt decides the answer on           46/150 = 30.7%

two variants disagree on: median 12.0% of reviews, max 28.7%
```

**On three reviews in ten, the answer is determined by the prompt's
formatting rather than by the review.** The model has an opinion on 69.3% of
this corpus; on the rest, what you get depends on whether you wrote a bulleted
list or a paragraph.

### What that means for everything else you measure

Put this next to @sec-classification's result on the same model family. There,
writing the instruction in English rather than Turkish — the single most
repeated piece of prompting folklore — was worth **+0.54 macro-F1, $p =
0.54$**, indistinguishable from nothing. Here, changing the *bullet
formatting* is worth eight points.

[The variable everyone argues about turned out to be noise, and the variable
nobody mentions turned out to be the largest effect in the experiment.]{.hl}

Three consequences, and the third is the one that changes how you work:

1. **A single-prompt model comparison is unreliable.** If prompt variance on
   one model is 14.67 points, then "model A beat model B by 5 points" measured
   with one prompt each is a statement about the prompts. Compare models over a
   *set* of prompts and report the distribution, or accept that you have not
   compared the models.
2. **Your reported accuracy needs an error bar you have not been computing.**
   The sampling interval on 150 documents is about ±6 points. The *prompt*
   interval, on the same data, is 14.67. The second is larger and almost never
   reported.
3. **Prompt changes need regression tests, not review.** No reviewer reading
   "moved the review above the instruction" would predict −4 points, because
   the change is semantically empty. Only a measurement catches it, which is
   what makes this a testing problem rather than a writing problem.

::: {.column-margin}
@sclar2024quantifying is the systematic version of this experiment across
tasks and models, and it finds the same thing at scale: spurious formatting
features move scores by amounts comparable to real model differences.
@lu2022fantastically found the same for the *order* of demonstrations. The
literature has been clear about this for years; the practice has not caught
up, because the prompt still feels like a message rather than a component.
:::

### The patterns that lost

Two results in that table are worth naming because they contradict widely
taught advice.

**The role prefix came 11th of 12** (76.00%, against 79.33% for the same
prompt without it). *You are an experienced customer-feedback analyst* is the
most reproduced prompting pattern in circulation, and on this task it cost
three points.

**Politeness cost 2.66 points.** *Lütfen… Teşekkürler* is harmless-looking and
it is not free.

Neither result generalises — that is the point. They are two more variables
that a competent reader would call irrelevant and the model does not. The
lesson is not "never use a role prefix"; it is that [you cannot tell which
prompt is better by reading them]{.hl}, and the belief that you can is what
this whole section is arguing against.

## Making prompt work reviewable {#sec-prompting-eval}

If the prompt is a component and its effect is 14.67 points, it needs the
machinery any other component gets. Four pieces, in the order they pay off.

### 1. Pin down reproducibility first

Before measuring anything, find out whether your setup returns the same answer
twice. Thirty reviews, ten repeats each:

```text
setting                          identical output   documents that varied
temperature 0, fixed seed              100.0%              0 / 30
temperature 0, no seed                 100.0%              0 / 30
temperature 0.7, fixed seed            100.0%              0 / 30
temperature 0.7, no seed                 3.3%             29 / 30
```

Good news and a trap. **Temperature 0 was deterministic here with or without a
seed, and a fixed seed made even temperature 0.7 deterministic.** But without
either, 29 of 30 documents gave a different answer across ten runs — so an
evaluation run at default settings is measuring the sampler as much as the
prompt.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
That table is a single local server answering one request at a time. **Hosted
APIs are frequently not deterministic even at temperature 0**, because
requests are batched and batch composition changes the order of floating-point
reductions. Do not assume; run the ten-repeat check against the endpoint you
will actually ship on, and if it is not deterministic, your eval needs repeats
and an interval rather than a single number.
:::

### 2. Build a small evaluation set, and freeze it

Fifty to two hundred items, labelled by you, covering the failure modes you
have already seen. It does not need to be large — it needs to be *fixed*, so
that two prompt versions are comparable.

The discipline from @sec-classification applies unchanged: hold it out, look at
it as rarely as possible, and never tune a prompt against the same items you
report on. A prompt tuned on its evaluation set is exactly as overfitted as a
model tuned on its test set, and far easier to do by accident because iterating
on a prompt feels like writing rather than fitting.

### 3. Compare paired, not independently

This is the statistical point @sec-prompting-brittle turned on. Two prompts run
on the *same* items are a paired comparison, so use the pairing: count the
documents where they disagree, and test that count.

```text
prompt A right, B wrong     32
prompt B right, A wrong     10
                            --
McNemar exact            p = 0.0009
```

Comparing two accuracy figures with overlapping confidence intervals would
have called that inconclusive. The paired test calls it decisively, from the
same 150 documents, because it throws away the 108 items both prompts agree
on — which carry no information about the difference.

### 4. Version the template, not the string

Store the template with slots, in the repository, with a version. Log which
version produced each output. When something regresses, the question *which
prompt was this* has to have an answer, and "the one in the notebook" is not
one.

```python
PROMPTS = {
    "sentiment/v3": "...",     # bulleted, labels positive/negative
    "sentiment/v4": "...",     # + explicit null case
}
```

Two habits that fall out of it: the assembled prompt is a *build artefact* and
should not be edited by hand, and a prompt change ships with its evaluation
delta the way a code change ships with tests.

## Intuition checks {#sec-prompting-intuition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Model A beat model B by 5 points on your eval. Which is better?

You do not know, because you have not separated the model from the prompt.
Measured on one model, one task and twelve semantically identical prompts, the
spread was **14.67 points** — three times the gap you are trying to interpret.

Run both models over a *set* of prompts and compare the distributions. If that
is too expensive, at least run each model on two or three prompts and report
the range. A single-prompt comparison is a statement about the prompts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your reviewer says "moving the input above the instruction is a no-op." Are they right?

Semantically yes, empirically no: it cost **4.00 points** here (79.33% → 75.33%).

That is the whole argument for treating prompts as testable components. No
reviewer can predict that by reading, because there is nothing to read — the
change is meaning-preserving. The only thing that catches it is running the
evaluation, which makes prompt changes a testing problem rather than a writing
problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Does "You are an expert…" help?

On this task it came 11th of 12, at 76.00% against 79.33% for the same prompt
without it.

Do not over-read that either — it is one task and one model, and the point is
not that role prefixes are bad. The point is that the most-reproduced pattern
in prompting lost to its own baseline here, and nobody would have guessed the
sign. Measure it on your task; it takes one extra run.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your few-shot examples have wrong labels. How bad is that?

Less bad than you would think, which tells you something about what
demonstrations are for. @min2022rethinking randomised the labels in the
demonstrations and most of the benefit survived, because what the examples
mainly convey is the *format and the label space* rather than the mapping.

Practical readings: do not spend a week hand-curating examples before checking
whether examples help at all; and if your task's difficulty is in the mapping
rather than the format, expect demonstrations to underdeliver.

What does move the number is *which* examples you show — @liu2022makes found
that retrieving demonstrations semantically close to the input beats a fixed
hand-picked set, which turns example selection into a retrieval problem and
hands it to @sec-retrieval's machinery.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Is temperature 0 reproducible?

Locally, here, yes — 100% identical across ten repeats, with or without a
seed. On a hosted API, often not, because batching changes floating-point
reduction order and your request shares a batch with strangers.

Run the check rather than assuming: same prompt, same input, ten times,
against the endpoint you will ship on. If it varies, every number in your
evaluation needs repeats and an interval.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When should a prompt stop being a prompt?

When you are maintaining a specification rather than writing a request. The
signals: the prompt has a version history, its output is parsed by code, a
change to it can break a downstream consumer, and you cannot safely edit it
without running something.

At that point it is a component of your system and belongs under the same
discipline as the rest of your code — repository, version, contract,
regression test. @sec-decoding is where the output contract gets *enforced*
rather than requested.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-prompting-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: What actually happens when you put examples in a prompt?**

Nothing is learned in the training sense — no weight changes and nothing
survives the call. The examples narrow which task the model performs, which is
why it is better described as task inference than as learning. Then deliver
the result that shows you have read past the tutorial: @min2022rethinking
randomised the demonstration labels and most of the benefit survived, so what
examples largely convey is the format and label space rather than the mapping.

**Q: Why did prompting stop feeling like a trick?**

Because instruction tuning happened. A base model continues text, so early
prompting meant constructing a prefix whose natural continuation was the
answer. Instruction tuning (@sec-post-training) trained models to treat an
instruction as an instruction. Candidates who cannot separate "the model got
bigger" from "the model got trained to follow instructions" have not thought
about where the capability came from.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Two prompts, which is better?**

Run both on the same frozen evaluation set and use a **paired** test — count
the items where they disagree and test that count, not the two accuracies.
Measured here, two prompts with overlapping confidence intervals were
separated at $p = 0.0009$ by McNemar, because the pairing discards the items
both got right.

If the answer is "I read them and the second is clearer", the candidate has
not measured a prompt.

**Q: How much of your reported accuracy is the prompt?**

The honest answer is that most teams do not know, and the measurement is a
morning's work: write several semantically identical prompts and run all of
them. Here twelve of them spanned **14.67 points**, and all twelve agreed on
only **69.3%** of items — so on three items in ten the formatting decided the
output. That number is an error bar that almost nobody reports and that is
usually larger than the sampling interval.

**Q: How do you stop prompt changes from breaking production?**

Treat the prompt as a versioned component: template in the repository, version
logged with every output, a frozen evaluation set, and a delta reported with
every change. Then say why review is not enough — a semantically empty edit
cost 4 points here and no reviewer would have predicted it.

**Q: Your evaluation results changed and nothing was deployed. What happened?**

Check reproducibility before anything else. Same prompt, same input, ten
repeats. Locally, temperature 0 was fully deterministic here; without a seed
at temperature 0.7, 29 of 30 items varied. And hosted endpoints are often
non-deterministic even at temperature 0, because batching changes
floating-point reduction order — so the answer may be that nothing happened
and your eval never had an interval on it.

| Python stdlib | 3.14.5 | the experiment is a `for` loop over prompts and a paired test; it needed no framework |

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|

| `dspy` | 3.3.1 | stops you writing prompt strings at all: declare the signature, let it compile the prompt against a metric. The right answer once you accept that hand-tuning a brittle artefact is a poor use of a week |
| `instructor` / `pydantic` | 1.15.4 / 2.13.4 | the output contract of @sec-prompting-spec as a Python type, validated on arrival |
| `guidance` | 0.3.1 | constrains generation to a template or grammar — @sec-decoding's machinery, applied at the prompt layer |
| `jinja2` | 3.1.6 | prompt templates with slots, versioned as files. Unglamorous, and it solves the "which prompt produced this" problem outright |
| `langsmith` | 0.11.1 | tracing and dataset management when the pipeline outgrows a spreadsheet |
| `pytest` | 9.1.1 | the point being that a prompt regression suite is just tests, and needs no LLM-specific framework to start |

: The wider ecosystem, versions as of writing {tbl-colwidths="[22,16,62]"}

::: {.column-margin}
`dspy` deserves the second look its position does not give it. Its premise is
exactly this chapter's finding: if prompt wording moves the score by amounts
you cannot predict, then hand-writing prompts is optimisation by guesswork,
and a compiler with a metric will beat you. The cost is that your prompts stop
being readable artefacts, which is a real trade rather than a free win.
:::

## Lab: turn a prompt into a component {#sec-prompting-lab}

Take a task you actually do — one where you have been iterating on a prompt by
feel. The lab converts it into something with a version and an error bar.

### Step 1 — freeze fifty items

Label them yourself. Include the failures you already know about; that is what
makes the set useful rather than decorative. Write them to a file and stop
editing it.

### Step 2 — measure reproducibility before anything else

Same prompt, same input, ten repeats, against the endpoint you will ship on.
If the answers vary, every number below needs repeats and an interval, and you
need to know that now rather than after a confusing week.

### Step 3 — write six prompts that mean the same thing

Not six *better* prompts — six that a colleague would call identical. Vary
formatting, label surface form, delimiters, the position of the input, a role
prefix. Run all six.

The spread you get is your prompt's error bar. Write it down; it is the number
that tells you how seriously to take every comparison you have made so far.

### Step 4 — pick the winner with a paired test

Best against worst, McNemar on the disagreements. Report the number of items
where they differ, not just the two accuracies.

### Step 5 — rewrite the winner as a specification

Output contract, explicit failure value, constraints near the end. Re-run.
Report whether the score moved and whether the *parse* failures went to zero,
which is usually the larger win.

### Step 6 — put it under version control and break it on purpose

Template with slots in a file, version string logged with each output. Then
make a semantically empty edit — reorder two sentences — and run the
evaluation. If the number moves, you have just demonstrated to yourself why
this is a testing problem.

### What to hand in

The six-prompt spread, the paired test for your winner, the before-and-after
for the specification rewrite, and one paragraph on what your prompt's error
bar means for the model comparison you most recently believed.

## Exercises {#sec-prompting-exercises}

1. **Your own brittleness number.** Six semantically identical prompts, one
   task, one model. Report the spread and the fraction of items where all six
   agree. Compare the spread against the difference between the two models you
   are choosing between.

2. **Paired versus unpaired.** Take two prompts whose confidence intervals
   overlap. Compute an unpaired comparison and a McNemar test on the same
   data. Report both, and say which you would put in a report and why.

3. **Randomise the demonstration labels.** Reproduce @min2022rethinking on your
   task: few-shot with correct labels, with shuffled labels, and zero-shot.
   How much of the benefit survives randomisation? What does the answer tell
   you about what your examples are doing?

4. **The role prefix, on your task.** Run the same prompt with and without
   *You are an expert…*. Predict the sign before you run it. Report both.

5. **Reproducibility on your endpoint.** Ten repeats at temperature 0 against a
   hosted API and against a local model. If they differ, explain the mechanism
   to a colleague in two sentences.

6. **Request to specification.** Take a prompt written as a request, rewrite it
   as a contract with an explicit failure value, and count parse failures
   before and after. Then find an input where the failure value is the correct
   answer and check that the model actually returns it.

7. **The regression you cannot see.** Make a meaning-preserving edit to a
   production prompt — reorder sentences, change bullets to prose. Run your
   evaluation. If nothing moved, try three more edits before concluding your
   task is robust.

## What to remember {#sec-prompting-summary}

- **In-context learning is task inference, not learning.** No weight changes
  and nothing survives the call. @min2022rethinking randomised the labels in
  the demonstrations and most of the benefit remained, which says examples
  mainly convey format and label space rather than the mapping.

- **The prompt is part of the model.** Twelve prompts that a competent reader
  would call the same instruction spanned **14.67 accuracy points** on one
  model and one task — 75.33% to 90.00%. That is not a writing difference; it
  is a component with an effect size.

- **On 30.7% of items, the prompt decided the answer.** All twelve variants
  agreed on only 69.3% of the reviews; two variants disagreed on a median of
  12% and as much as 28.7%. Your model has an opinion on most items and the
  formatting decides the rest.

- **The spread is real, and paired testing is how you show it.** Best against
  worst: overlapping confidence intervals, 42 disagreements, McNemar
  **$p = 0.0009$**. Comparing two accuracies would have called it
  inconclusive; the pairing throws away the 108 items that carry no
  information and finds the signal.

- **Which means a single-prompt model comparison is unreliable.** If prompt
  variance is 14.67 points, "model A beat model B by 5" measured with one
  prompt each is a statement about prompts. Compare over a set of prompts and
  report the distribution.

- **The folklore variable was noise and the ignored one was the effect.**
  @sec-classification measured English-versus-Turkish instructions at
  **+0.54, $p = 0.54$** on this model family. Bullet formatting, here, was
  worth eight points. The role prefix — the most reproduced pattern in
  circulation — came 11th of 12 and cost 3.33 points against its own baseline.

- **You cannot tell which prompt is better by reading them.** That is the whole
  case for treating prompt changes as a testing problem: a semantically empty
  edit cost 4.00 points, and no reviewer would have predicted the sign.

- **Check reproducibility before you measure anything.** Locally, temperature 0
  was fully deterministic with or without a seed, and a fixed seed made even
  temperature 0.7 deterministic — but with neither, 29 of 30 items varied
  across ten runs. Hosted APIs are frequently non-deterministic even at
  temperature 0, because batching changes floating-point reduction order. Run
  the ten-repeat check on the endpoint you will ship on.

- **Write prompts as specifications.** Name the output contract, name the
  failure value, and put constraints where they bind. Then validate the
  contract — a schema you do not check is a comment, and @sec-summarization
  already showed that a schema guarantees shape and never truth.
